newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish forces withdrawing from northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkish forces withdrawing from northern Iraq.

text.p: Turkish forces are withdrawing in large numbers from northern Iraq after a month-long foray into the area in pursuit of Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) separatist rebels, witnesses said.
Over 100 armoured vehicles plus large numbers of troops have crossed the Turkish-Iraqi border at the main road crossing at Habur in the last three days, the witnesses said.

Sources close to the rebels confirmed the troops withdrawal and said that rebels had retaken the strategic Zap valley from the Turkish army which Turkey had said was the PKK's headquarters in the area.
Turkey said that it would withdraw from northern Iraq once the operation was over and the region was under the control of their Iraqi Kurd allies, the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).

A spokesman for the Kurdish language Med TV based in Belgium told Reuters that PKK guerrillas had attacked KDP forces left guarding the Zap valley at Kurijahro on Saturday and were now in complete control of the area.
Four KDP fighters and two Turkish soldiers were killed in clashes in northern Iraq on Saturday, the spokesman said. No details of PKK casualties were given.

Two soldiers were killed and four soldiers injured in a rebel rocket attack on a freight train in Bingol province of southeast Turkey, state-run Anatolian news agency said on Sunday. It did not say when the attack took place.
More than 10,000 Turkish troops streamed into northern Iraq on May 14 in pursuit of PKK rebels, who have fought the military since 1984 for self-rule in southeast Turkey.
The Turkish military says it has killed around 2,500 rebels for the loss of about 100 soldiers since the operation started, while the PKK says it has killed around 800 soldiers.
The operation, carried out under a strict news blackout, has drawn criticism from NATO member Turkey's Western allies and countries in the Middle East.

The Arab League secretariat has condemned the incursion, calling for the withdrawal of troops from the so-called Kurdish "safe haven", set up after the Gulf War in 1991 to protect the local population from attacks by Baghdad.
Turkey has blamed Iran, Syria and other countries for providing the PKK with sophisticated weaponry, including shoulder-fired SA-7 missiles used to shoot down two Turkish helicopters.
